344.title: The flood (Genesis 7)
344.hook: the fountains of the deep break open, and God remembers Noah
344.tomorrow: The dove and the olive leaf
344.howItsDone: Some churches pray for those in trouble by name each week, and the first letter of Peter links the flood to baptism, so some churches read the story at the Easter Vigil and recall it in baptism prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ark, a box built on dry land, and your line was build anyway. Did you put in one plank on the thing others doubt? Day three hundred forty-four.

Go back to the very first page. Darkness on the face of the deep. Waters everywhere. Then God divides them: a dome to hold the waters above, seas gathered so dry land can appear. Creation, in Genesis, is partly a story of water being given its place. Now, in chapter seven, the story runs that film backwards. The waters come back. Up from below, down from above. The dry land disappears. It's as if the world is being unmade, returned to the deep. And inside a wooden box, floating on all of it, are Noah, his family, and the animals. Today is the flood, and one small word in the middle of it.
screen: `CREATION: WATER GIVEN ITS PLACE.` → `THE FILM RUNS BACKWARDS.` → `A BOX ON THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's how the King James Bible tells it: "the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened." The deep from verse two of the Bible, and the waters above the dome from day nine, both let loose at once. Rain for forty days and forty nights. The waters rise over the mountains, and stay for a hundred and fifty days. Two small details are worth knowing. First, the animals. Two by two is the famous version. But chapter seven also tells Noah to take the clean animals, and the birds, by sevens. Both are in the text. Second, after everyone is inside, there's this: "and the LORD shut him in." Noah doesn't close the door. God does. Then the long, long wait, in the dark, in the noise, with no land anywhere. And at the turn, the first verse of the next chapter: "And God remembered Noah." In Hebrew, zakhar, to remember. It doesn't mean God had forgotten. Here, God's remembering is the hinge. Right after it, a wind passes over the earth, like the Spirit over the waters at the start, and the waters begin to go down. Christians read the flood in different ways: some as a worldwide event, some as a regional flood remembered in a great story, some as a story whose truth is about God and people more than geology. Other ancient peoples told flood stories too. However it's read, the text turns on three words: God remembered Noah.
screen: `THE FOUNTAINS OF THE DEEP BROKEN UP.` · `TWO BY TWO, AND BY SEVENS.` · `THE LORD SHUT HIM IN.` · `ZAKHAR: TO REMEMBER IS TO ACT.` · then, large: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who's in deep water. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person who's in over their head right now. Grief, illness, debt, a marriage coming apart, a long dark wait with no land in sight. Picture them clearly, wherever they are this evening. Hold them in mind the way the story says God held Noah. Not just a passing thought. Remembering that leads somewhere. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. After the bell, think of one small act that could follow. The bell holds the time.
The flood. The waters of the first page let loose again, the world almost unmade, and in the middle, the turn: God remembered Noah.
Your line: god remembers. Today, turn remembering into one act for the person in deep water: a message, a meal, a visit. Day three hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 344 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOVE AND THE OLIVE LEAF.`

345.title: The dove and the olive leaf (Genesis 8:6–12)
345.hook: the raven doesn't return; the dove comes back with a leaf
345.howItsDone: The dove appears across Christian art as a sign of the Holy Spirit and of peace, and in the catacombs of Rome early Christians drew a dove with an olive branch on tombs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flood, the world almost unmade, and the turn when God remembered Noah. Your line was god remembers. Did you turn remembering into one act? Day three hundred forty-five.

Before radar and satellites, sailors lost at sea sometimes carried birds on board. When they couldn't see land, they'd let one go and watch. If it circled and came back, there was no shore within reach. If it flew off in a straight line, they followed it. The ark has been floating for months. The rain has stopped, the waters are going down, the box has come to rest on the mountains of Ararat. But Noah can't see out. There's one window, and all he can see through it is sky. So he does what those sailors did. He opens the window, and lets a bird go.
screen: `SAILORS LOST AT SEA, A BIRD ON BOARD.` → `THE ARK RESTS ON ARARAT.` → `NOAH OPENS THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: The first bird is a raven. In the King James Bible, it "went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth." It never comes back with news. Ravens can live on what they find, even in a drowned world. Then Noah sends a dove. She finds nowhere to rest her foot, and comes back. And there's a tender detail here: Noah puts out his hand, and takes her, and pulls her in. A man who hasn't said a word in the whole story, reaching out the window for a tired bird. He waits seven days. He sends her again. And this time: "And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth." One leaf. Not a field, not a forest, not dry ground under his feet. Just a single fresh leaf in a bird's beak. Olive trees are tough; they can come back from almost nothing. And that leaf is enough for Noah to know. Something is growing again out there. He waits seven more days, sends her one last time, and she doesn't come back at all. Which is good news too: she's found a home. In Hebrew, dove is yonah, the same as the prophet Jonah's name. And for Christians, the dove will return at the Jordan River, when the Spirit comes down on Jesus at his baptism like a dove. Centuries later, the dove with an olive branch became a picture of peace across the world. It started with one leaf at evening.
screen: `THE RAVEN GOES TO AND FRO.` · `NOAH PULLS THE DOVE IN.` · `ONE OLIVE LEAF.` · `YONAH: THE DOVE FOUND A HOME.` · then, large: `IN HER MOUTH WAS AN OLIVE LEAF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for one sign of hope. Settle, and breathe. Think about the situation in your life that still feels underwater. Don't look for the whole answer. Don't look for dry land. Look for a leaf. One small thing that's growing again: a better morning, a kind word, a bill paid, a doctor's good news, one honest conversation. It may be very small. That's fine. Hold it in your mind like Noah held that leaf. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Yonah. The Hebrew word for dove, the same as the prophet Jonah's name: the bird that came back with one green leaf.
Your line: a leaf is enough. Today, tell one person about a small sign of hope you've seen, theirs or yours, before the whole thing is fixed. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: The rainbow (Genesis 9:8–17)
346.hook: God hangs up his bow in the clouds: never again
346.howItsDone: Covenant runs through Christian teaching, from the promise to Noah to the new covenant Jesus names at the Last Supper, and churches recall the new covenant at communion, in Jesus' words over the cup.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dove, yonah, and the olive leaf, one small sign that something was growing again, and your line was a leaf is enough. Who did you tell about a sign of hope? Day three hundred forty-six.

When two old enemies make peace, there's often a gesture. Swords laid on a table. A flag lowered. A gun handed over and never picked up again. Something you can see that says: this is over. Noah's family has stepped out of the ark onto a scrubbed, silent earth. Everything they knew is gone. They've just lived through the flood, and the next time a storm cloud rolls in, they might wonder. So God speaks, not only to Noah, but past him, to everything that breathes. And God makes a gesture you can still see after a summer storm.
screen: `SWORDS LAID ON A TABLE.` → `A SCRUBBED, SILENT EARTH.` → `A GESTURE YOU CAN STILL SEE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is covenant. In Hebrew, berit. It's a binding promise between two parties, the kind of solemn agreement that holds a family, a nation or a marriage together. This one is unusual. Listen to who it's with: Noah, his sons, their children after them, and every living creature, the birds, the cattle, every beast of the earth. Not just people. Animals too. And listen to what it asks of them. Nothing. There are no conditions on this side of it. God simply binds himself: "neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth." Then the sign, in the King James Bible: "I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth." The Hebrew word for rainbow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a bow, the weapon, the kind a warrior draws. Some readers picture it this way: God hanging the war bow up in the sky, unstrung, pointed away from the earth. Then a question: who is the sign for? You'd think it's for us, to calm us down when the clouds come. But God says, I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant. The rainbow is a token for the earth, and a reminder God sets for himself. The same word as the flood's turning point: God remembers. Christians have gone on to speak of other covenants in the Bible, with Abraham, at Sinai, and the new covenant at the Last Supper. They start here, with every living thing, and a bow hung in the clouds.
screen: `BERIT: A BINDING PROMISE.` · `WITH EVERY LIVING CREATURE.` · `QESHET: A WARRIOR'S BOW.` · `A REMINDER GOD SETS FOR HIMSELF.` · then, large: `I DO SET MY BOW IN THE CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for color in the sky. If you're near a window, look out at the sky. If not, picture the last sky you saw. Notice whatever color is in it: gray, blue, the orange at the edge of evening, the white of a cloud. Let your eyes rest there. Then think of a promise that someone keeps to you without asking anything back. A parent, a friend, a stranger's kindness. If you pray, you can give thanks for promises kept. The bell holds the time.
Covenant. Berit in Hebrew, a binding promise. This one is made with every living creature, sealed with a bow in the clouds.
Your line: never again. Today, look up at the sky at least once, and if there's a promise you've broken, decide on one never again of your own. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
347.hook: humans build a tower to make a name for themselves, and languages scatter
347.carry: no need to make a name
347.howItsDone: Some churches read the Babel story at Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, and some read the Pentecost lesson aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, covenant, a bow hung up in the clouds as a promise to every living thing, and your line was never again. Did you look up at the sky? Day three hundred forty-seven.

A ribbon cutting, a light show, a name in giant letters at the top of a new tower, so everyone driving into the city knows who built it. Building high to be seen is an old idea. In Genesis, after the flood, people move east and settle on a plain in the land of Shinar. Some readers picture the stepped towers of baked brick, called ziggurats, whose ruins still stand in that part of the world. Everyone speaks one language. And they have a new technology, and a big idea.
screen: `A NAME IN LIGHTS ON A NEW TOWER.` → `A PLAIN IN THE LAND OF SHINAR.` → `ONE LANGUAGE, A BIG IDEA.`

segments.voice: The technology is brick. In the King James Bible: "they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter." Slime is bitumen, tar. Fired bricks and tar: a way to build high. And the big idea, verse four: "let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth." Make us a name. That's the heart of it. Not a temple to honor God. A monument to themselves, so they'd never be scattered. And remember, after the flood, God had told Noah's family to fill the earth. They want to stay put, and be famous. Then comes a line with a smile in it: "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." A tower meant to reach heaven, and God has to come down to see it. From heaven, it's tiny. So God confuses their language, and they stop building, and they scatter. And the city gets its name. In Hebrew, Babel sounds like balal, to mix up, to confuse. The text is enjoying the pun: Babel, the name of the great city Babylon, is tied here to confusion. Some Christians read the story alongside Pentecost in the book of Acts, when the Spirit comes and people from many nations each hear the apostles in their own language. Babel scatters the languages; Pentecost gathers people without erasing them. And there's one more contrast, coming tomorrow: they wanted to make a name. Tomorrow, God offers to make one.
screen: `BRICK FOR STONE, TAR FOR MORTAR.` · `LET US MAKE US A NAME.` · `GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.` · `BABEL, BALAL: MIXED UP.` · then, large: `LET US MAKE US A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing without needing credit. Settle, and breathe. Notice where your day goes into making a name: the post, the reply-all, the story told so you come out well. No judgment; just notice. Now think of one good thing you could do today where nobody will ever know it was you. Refill the coffee. Pay a compliment about someone behind their back. Fix the thing quietly. Picture doing it, and walking away. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Babel. A tower meant to reach heaven, built to make a name, and the city named for what happened next: balal, mixed up.
Your line: no need to make a name. Today, do one good thing where nobody will know it was you, and don't tell anyone after. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: Go (Genesis 12:1–9)
348.hook: at seventy-five, Abram is told to leave for a land he'll be shown
348.howItsDone: Christian tradition calls Abraham a father of faith, and his call to go is read at some commissioning services, when people are sent out to new work, a new place or a mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babel, a tower built so small God had to come down to see it, and your line was no need to make a name. What did you do that nobody will know was you? Day three hundred forty-eight.

Seventy-five. By then, the furniture is where it is. The friends are the friends. The doctor knows your name. Abram is seventy-five, living in a city called Haran, with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything they own. Sarai, the text has already told us, cannot have children. Up to now, Genesis has moved fast, whole generations in a verse. Now it slows down and zooms in on one old man. Because God is about to speak to him, and the story turns on what he does next.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, SETTLED IN HARAN.` → `GENESIS ZOOMS IN ON ONE MAN.` → `THEN GOD SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's how it begins in the King James Bible: "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee." In Hebrew, the first words are lekh lekha: go, and a little extra word that can mean for yourself, or even to yourself. Some Jewish teachers read it as a journey outward that is also a journey inward. Notice the order of what he has to leave. Country, then relatives, then his father's house. Each one closer, each one harder. And notice what's missing: the destination. A land that I will show you. No map, no name. Then the promise, and remember Babel. The people of Babel said, let us make us a name. Here God says to Abram: I will make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing. What they tried to grab, Abram is given. And not just for himself: in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. The blessing is meant to spill over. Then one plain sentence: "So Abram departed." And "Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran." He goes. Along the way, he builds altars. Much later, the letter to the Hebrews sums it up: he went out, not knowing whither he went. Jews and Muslims honor Abraham too, as a father in faith. And Christians often call him that: the one who went, before he knew where.
screen: `LEKH LEKHA: GO, FOR YOURSELF.` · `COUNTRY, KIN, FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `NO MAP, NO NAME.` · `WHAT BABEL GRABBED, ABRAM IS GIVEN.` · then, large: `SO ABRAM DEPARTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step without the whole map. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been waiting to start until you can see the whole way through. A conversation, an application, a move, a change, a first visit somewhere new. Notice how much you want the map first. Now ask a smaller question: what is the first step, just the first one? Picture yourself taking it, not knowing the rest. If you pray, you can ask for courage for that one step. The bell holds the time.
Go. Lekh lekha in Hebrew. The word that sends Abram, at seventy-five, out of his country toward a land he'll be shown.
Your line: go, not knowing. Today, take the first step you pictured, even if you can't see the second one yet. Day three hundred forty-eight.

349.title: Lot chooses the plain (Genesis 13)
349.hook: Abram lets his nephew pick first, and Lot picks what looks best
349.howItsDone: Some Christians read Abram's choice as a picture of peacemaking and humility, and his words 'let there be no strife… for we be brethren' are quoted when families or churches work through disputes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, go: Abram at seventy-five, leaving for a land he'd be shown, and your line was go, not knowing. Did you take the first step you pictured? Day three hundred forty-nine.

Two families share a vacation rental. On the first night there are two bedrooms: one with a sea view and a big bed, one by the laundry room with bunks. Somebody has to choose. What follows is a small dance of politeness. Abram and his nephew Lot have a bigger version of that problem. They've both done well. Too well. So many sheep, goats and cattle that the land can't feed them all, and their herdsmen have started quarreling. Something has to give. Abram is the older one, the head of the family. The choice is his to make. And he doesn't make it.
screen: `TWO BEDROOMS, ONE WITH A VIEW.` → `TOO MANY FLOCKS, QUARRELING HERDERS.` → `THE CHOICE IS ABRAM'S.`

segments.voice: Here's what Abram says, in the King James Bible: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren." We're family. Then: "Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left." The older man, the one with every right to choose first, hands the choice to the younger. And Lot looks. He "lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where." The text compares it to the garden of the LORD. Green, rich, easy. It's the obvious choice, and he takes it. The Hebrew word for that plain, kikkar, means something round: a circle of land, the same word used for a round loaf, and for a talent, that heavy round weight of silver from the parable. A lot of value in one circle. But then the text adds a quiet warning: Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom, and "the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly." Choosing by what looks best has a cost the eyes can't see yet. And Abram, left with the hill country? Right after Lot leaves, God tells him: lift up your eyes. Look north, south, east and west. All of it, to you and your children. Lot lifted his eyes and grabbed. Abram is told to lift his and receive. The text doesn't call Lot a villain; he's family, and he'll be rescued more than once. But it lets you see two ways of choosing.
screen: `NO STRIFE: WE BE BRETHREN.` · `THE OLDER LETS THE YOUNGER CHOOSE.` · `KIKKAR: A RICH, ROUND PLAIN.` · `TOWARD SODOM.` · then, large: `IS NOT THE WHOLE LAND BEFORE THEE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone else choose first. Settle, and breathe. Think about the small choices coming up in the next day: the last slice, the seat in the car, the TV show, the parking space, which project you take. Pick one where you'd normally choose first, and imagine handing it over. Notice what you feel: relief, a twinge of loss, a little pride. Notice whether anything is actually at risk. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Kikkar. The Hebrew word for the round, well-watered plain Lot chose at a glance, pitching his tent toward Sodom.
Your line: you choose first. Today, say it out loud once, about something small, and mean it. Day three hundred forty-nine.

350.title: Melchizedek (Genesis 14:17–20)
350.hook: a mysterious priest-king brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram
350.howItsDone: Many Christians remember Melchizedek at communion: the Roman Canon of the Catholic Mass names his offering, and the letter to the Hebrews, read in many churches, calls Jesus a priest after his order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lot chose the plain, the kikkar, the green land that looked best, and your line was you choose first. Did you hand over a choice, and mean it? Day three hundred fifty, the end of the week.

Lot's green plain didn't stay peaceful. Chapter fourteen is a war story: four kings against five, armies sweeping through the Jordan valley, and Lot carried off as a captive with everything he owns. Abram hears, gathers three hundred eighteen men from his own household, chases the raiders north by night, and brings Lot back, with the people and the goods. He comes home a victor. And as he does, two kings come out to meet him. One is the king of Sodom, who wants to make a deal. The other comes out of nowhere, says almost nothing, and then vanishes from the story.
screen: `FOUR KINGS AGAINST FIVE.` → `ABRAM BRINGS LOT BACK.` → `TWO KINGS COME OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Here he is, in the King James Bible: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God." A king, and a priest, both at once. Salem is usually taken to be an early name for Jerusalem, and in Hebrew it sounds like shalom, peace. His own name, Malki-tsedeq, means my king is righteousness. He blesses Abram: "Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth." And Abram gives him a tenth of everything, the first tithe in the Bible. Then Melchizedek is gone. No parents named, no birth, no death, no other appearance in Genesis. That silence is exactly what made him fascinating. A psalm, the hundred and tenth, speaks of a king who is "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." And the New Testament letter to the Hebrews, centuries later, builds a long argument on him: a priest without father, without mother, who points ahead, it says, to Jesus, a priest of a different order. And the bread and wine? Many Christians, especially Catholic and Orthodox, have seen in them an early sign of the Lord's Supper; the oldest Roman Mass prayer still names Melchizedek's offering. Others read it more simply, as a royal welcome of food for tired soldiers. Both readings start with the same scene: a stranger who belongs to no tribe we know, blessing Abram with a meal. That ends a week of water and fresh starts: the flood, a leaf, a bow in the clouds, a tower, a call to go, a choice, and now, bread and wine and blessing.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone with food. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone coming back from a battle of their own: a long shift, a hospital stay, a hard week, a move. Picture them walking in the door, tired. Now picture what you could put in their hands. Not a feast. Bread, soup, coffee, a sandwich, a box of something sweet. Plain food, offered with a good word. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on them. After the bell, decide who, and what. The bell holds the time.
Melchizedek. King of Salem and priest of the most high God, who meets Abram with bread and wine and a blessing, and then disappears.
